courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
md: Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: Being logged in is not a permission. Authentication tells the server *who* is asking; it says nothing about *which* objects and functions that person may touch. Each request needs both answers.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
md: Adding a login in front of an endpoint is not the fix for broken authorization. Peloton's partial fix and USPS's whole design show the result: every registered user, and anyone can register, gets everyone's data.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
md: Relay borrows a live NTLM sign-in instead of stealing a hash. It is stopped by binding authentication to the session or channel: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and EPA on HTTPS. Then remove the bait: LLMNR, NBT-NS and NTLM itself. To respond, isolate the rogue host, review what the relayed identity did on the target, and revoke any certificate issued through a relayed login.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: DCSync abuses a legitimate protocol: anyone with both replication rights can ask a DC for any password hash. Control who holds those rights, audit 4662 with the replication GUIDs, and treat a DCSync as compromise of every account.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Misconception: "we have CFI, so memory corruption cannot hurt us." CFI guards one rung. An attacker who already has arbitrary read/write can often reach the goal by changing data instead of code pointers (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Rules of engagement for a red team
md: Never let the red team decide alone that something is safe. Offensive actions have side effects that nobody planned: an old system that falls over when scanned, a test that locks out a service account. Two-person integrity, a named control-group contact who answers at 2 a.m., and a halt that works in minutes are cheaper than any of those outcomes.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: cracked Cobalt Strike and the takedowns
md: Do not write rules for a framework's defaults and call C2 covered. Malleable profiles exist precisely so that traffic can be made to look like something else, and CISA's federal red team ran more than seven different implants to prove the point (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
md: Checklist for any agent leaderboard number: which subset and version; which harness, tools, step and cost budget; one attempt or best of many (pass@k vs pass^1 vs pass^k); how many tasks and trials, with an interval; and whether the tasks predate the model's training cutoff.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: A memory system is defined by four decisions: what to write, how to reconcile it with what is already stored, what to retrieve for a given step, and what to forget. Retrieval alone is RAG; the write and forget decisions are what make it memory.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling
md: FPR sets the ceiling, TPR sets the speed. With enough samples, best-of-N accuracy converges to the verifier's precision $pt / (pt + (1-p)f)$. Raising TPR only means you need fewer samples to get there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Prompt injection: when data becomes instructions
md: Treat every token the model reads as a possible instruction from whoever wrote it. You cannot reliably make the model ignore it, so limit what obeying it can achieve.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: System prompt leakage and sensitive information disclosure
md: Assume the system prompt will be read by users and attackers. Put nothing in it that would hurt if published, and enforce every rule that matters in code.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
md: A crystal is a set of atom types, fractional coordinates in [0, 1), and a 3x3 lattice. Cartesian position is $f$ times $L$, coordinates wrap mod 1, and every distance must use the minimum image.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: A tiny false positive rate is not zero at scale. $z > 4$ means a one-sided p of $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$: scan a million human documents and expect about 32 false flags. Hugging Face's `WatermarkDetector` defaults to $z > 3$, where the rate is $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Pick the threshold for the cost of a false accusation.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: Misconception: "Sign in with X" means OAuth logged you in. Plain OAuth only says some client got a token. Building login on raw access tokens has caused real impersonation bugs; OpenID Connect adds the missing pieces.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Validation is a fixed checklist the receiver owns: pinned algorithm, trusted issuer's key, signature, iss, aud, exp and nbf with small leeway, type. A library helps only when you pass it every one of those rules.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
md: SDL says what one company does, SAMM measures how mature you are, and SSDF is the reference list that governments and customers ask you to attest to. Most programmes use SAMM to plan and SSDF to report. You will also meet BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model), which describes what real companies' programmes do rather than prescribing a target.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
md: Rewriting git history to remove a secret does not un-leak it. Forks, clones, CI caches and anyone who fetched in the meantime still have it. Treat any committed secret as compromised: rotate it, then look at the provider's logs for its use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Programme decisions: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design
md: Finding bugs is linear work; removing bug classes compounds. A mature programme spends part of its budget on defaults, paved roads and language choices that make the next thousand findings never happen.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Search is asymmetric. Queries and documents differ in length, form and role, and relevance means *answers*, not *looks like*. Tell the model which side each text is on.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
md: Retry with: honor Retry-After when present (plus a little randomness); otherwise capped exponential backoff with full jitter; a maximum number of attempts and a total time budget; and retries only for retryable errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), never for 400-class mistakes (4xx codes such as 400 Bad Request mean the request itself is wrong, so it fails the same way again), billing or quota errors.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
md: Forced periodic rotation makes passwords weaker, not stronger: people make the smallest possible change. CISA's advisory on Scattered Spider (a cybercriminal group that targets companies through their IT help desks, lesson 12) repeats NIST's advice to refrain from recurring password changes. Change on evidence of compromise instead.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
md: Identity attacks leave traces in authentication logs: failures, travel, new devices, MFA changes. Centralising login through SSO makes those traces easy to collect, and makes the IdP the account to protect most.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: `inferenceConfig` has only four fields. Putting a model-specific parameter there is a mistake; it belongs in `additionalModelRequestFields`, and it only works for models that define it.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
md: Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: Branchless code trades a *possible* misprediction for *always* doing the work of both sides plus the select. Always check the compiler output (Compiler Explorer, the godbolt.org website that shows the assembly a compiler produces, or the `-S` flag, which makes the compiler write assembly instead of an object file) before hand-rewriting: the optimizer may already have done it, or may have a good reason not to.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: Misconception: "LSM-trees have no write amplification because they only write sequentially." They write sequentially, but every byte is rewritten as it moves down levels: about 33x in RocksDB's leveled example. The win is in I/O pattern and batching, not in writing less, and on some workloads a B+tree writes fewer bytes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
md: Resilience is the outcome; continuity is about business processes; contingency and disaster recovery are about systems and sites. A real organisation needs a small family of plans that agree with each other on who decides, in what order things come back, and who speaks.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
md: Every backup needs an owner, a check on every step, an alert on missing success through a separate channel, and an automated restore test that measures time and verifies content. Rehearsed restores (Gmail 2011) produce estimates; unrehearsed ones (GitLab 2017) produce surprises.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
md: Draw the dependency graph of recovery itself and look for cycles. Break them with out-of-band copies (exported keys, printed runbooks, separate comms), break-glass accounts that depend on nothing in the estate, and tested access paths for every security tool you will need on the worst day.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
md: A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Learning where to cut: from character models to H-Net
md: The design space for byte models is who decides the cut: a fixed rate, a hand-written rule, a separate model (BLT), or the model's own loss (H-Net's cosine router plus a ratio loss). Learned cuts remove BLT's separately trained entropy model, at the cost of new machinery to make a discrete choice trainable.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Power-of-two strides are a trap. In this L1d every address 4096 bytes apart maps to the same set, and a set has only 8 ways. Walking a column of `double m[N][512]` (rows of exactly 4 KB) puts every line in one set: only 8 of them can be cached at once even though the cache holds 512 lines.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Cloud incident response reconstructs what identities did through the provider's API, across four evidence layers: control plane, data plane, workload and identity provider. What you can prove is decided before the incident, by which logs were on and where they were kept.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
md: Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level where the learned clause becomes unit and forces (asserts) its last literal + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
md: Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
md: The naive loop is slow for a scheduling reason, not a kernel reason. Three units that could run at once are being used one at a time. The rest of this course is the machinery for filling those holes: **pinned memory** (so copies can be asynchronous), **streams** (so work can be queued independently), **events** (so order is expressed without stalling), and **graphs** (so launching the work is cheap).

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: From [CLS] to a score: logits, sigmoid and monoT5's true token
md: Sigmoid is monotonic (a larger logit always gives a larger score), so it never changes the order of candidates. The Sentence Transformers docs say so explicitly: MS MARCO models return logits, and adding a Sigmoid activation gives 0 to 1 scores without changing the ranking. Use sigmoid when you need a threshold or a comparable confidence, not to improve ranking.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
md: Use an AEAD for every new design, generate a fresh nonce per message (a counter, or 12 random bytes with a usage limit), and treat a decrypt failure as an attack, never as "try again without checking".

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Unauthenticated encryption: why decryption must refuse first
md: Common misconception: "we check that the decrypted data is valid JSON, so tampering is detected". Parsing is not authentication. The parser runs on attacker-shaped plaintext, and its success or failure is one more signal the attacker can observe.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: MAC constructions: length extension, ambiguity and replay
md: Authenticate exactly the bytes you will act on, in an encoding with one meaning, including who signed it, for what purpose and when. HMAC (or keyed BLAKE2) answers "was this made with the key"; only your encoding answers "was it made for this".

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
md: Composition reshapes, divide tiles, slicing selects. local_tile picks a CTA's tile, local_partition or a TV layout picks a thread's share, and both are just layout algebra applied to the same tensor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
md: Pooling and sharing are different. In **pooling** each slice of memory belongs to exactly one host at a time; it just moves between hosts. In **sharing** (CXL 3.0) several hosts map the same bytes at once and hardware keeps them coherent. Most CXL disaggregation designs, including Pond, use pooling.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The CFAA: access, authorisation, damage and loss
md: CFAA in one line each: (a)(2) access without or beyond authorisation that obtains information; (a)(5) causing damage; (a)(7) extortion; (g) civil suits, usually needing USD 5,000 of loss in a year. Damage means impaired integrity or availability; loss includes the cost of responding.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
md: A good later career does not erase earlier conduct. Hutchins' defensive work counted heavily at sentencing, but the plea still followed. Statutes of limitation are long, and chat logs last.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
md: Do not 'clean up' logs before handing them over, even to remove noise. Any edit you cannot explain undermines everything else. Produce the original export and do analysis on a copy.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
md: The mixture is a vector of $k$ probabilities chosen **before** training, and it silently allocates billions of tokens. DoReMi's question: can we choose it automatically, cheaply, and without looking at downstream benchmarks?

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
md: A perplexity filter keeps text that resembles its reference corpus, not text that is good. Using Wikipedia as the reference quietly downweights dialects, jargon and informal writing. Thresholds should be checked by training models on the result, not set by eye.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: A common misconception, called out by Fabian himself: data-oriented design is not only about cache misses or splitting hot and cold fields. It is about designing around the data and the transforms on it. Layout is the most visible tool, not the whole method.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
md: Every query ability you add to encrypted data leaks something: deterministic encryption leaks equality and frequency, so never use it on low-cardinality columns. Enclaves add order: randomized columns that support range queries leak the order of values to anyone who can scan the index. They move trust from the administrator to the enclave and its attestation, and only SGX keeps out the host OS.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
md: Disposal is a chain of custody: inventory by serial number, sanitise to the data's classification, use vetted vendors, require a per-device certificate naming method, tool and verifier, and reconcile every serial. Read the certificates.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: A passing simulation is only as good as its fault model and its oracles. If your simulated disk never loses unsynced writes, you have not tested crash recovery; if no oracle checks liveness, a stuck cluster passes.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
md: Do not "fix" drift by blindly running apply from the drift job. The job holds a read-only role on purpose, and an automatic revert can undo an emergency change in the middle of an incident. Alert, decide, then go through the normal pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency): lesson 1's estimate gives an H100 room for about 295 tokens per pass at the cost of one. Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
md: A carved file has no name, no path, no timestamps and no owner. You can testify that these bytes were on the disk at this offset. Who created them, and when, needs other evidence.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
md: Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
md: Do not read DPO's $\beta$ as a guarantee of staying close to the reference. On pairs the model already separates, DPO's gradient shrinks but never pushes back, so drift continues as long as you keep training. The IPO paper notes that early stopping is the usual extra guard.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
md: A backfill copy is always an *old* view of a row. Whatever mechanism you use (insert-if-absent, versions, or watermarks), it must guarantee that a backfilled row can never land after a newer write for the same key, and that deletes are remembered.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
md: Probe context matters. `tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue` often fires in the context of the process that issued the I/O, but it can also fire from kernel context (for example readahead, where the kernel reads file pages before anyone asks for them), so `comm` and `pid` may not name the application you expect.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: A common misconception: "it is a security product, so it is secure". Firewalls and VPNs are software written under the same pressures as any other, and they run on the most exposed spot you have. KEV counts measure exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how widely a product is deployed; they are not a ranking of code quality.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
md: Mitigation is not remediation, and patching is not the end. For a KEV edge bug that is automatable or gives total control, assume exploitation may have come first: patch within days, then look for signs it already happened.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
md: The two papers do not agree on the exact mechanism. Fatemi et al. argue that the $1/|o_i|$ account is incomplete, because a longer response also adds more terms to the sum being divided. They agree on the direction that matters in practice: negative advantages pull toward longer responses, positive ones toward shorter. The share of wrong answers in training therefore steers length.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: Inference-time levers are cheap but blunt: forcing a stop interrupts reasoning, forcing 'Wait' saturates. Training-time methods (preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO) teach the model to plan a shorter trace, which is why L1 beats budget forcing at small budgets.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
md: Misconception: "a GrantedAccess of 0x1FFFFF on LSASS is always an attack." Security products, backup agents and admin tools often request all access. Context decides: which signed program, how often, from which path, and with which call trace. Baseline the normal requesters on your hosts, then alert on the rest.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: A service principal can hold an Entra admin role, and Microsoft names those that do as control plane assets. An app with Global Administrator, or with permission to assign roles, is a Global Administrator that has no MFA prompt to bypass. Review apps in role assignments with the same care as people.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Misconception: resetting a compromised user's password ends the attacker's access immediately. It revokes only refresh tokens obtained with the password (revoke sessions for the rest), and an access token already issued keeps working until it expires (up to 90 minutes) at any service that does not support CAE, and app sessions with their own cookies (the federation course's offboarding gap) are untouched.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: Misconception: 'We have Conditional Access requiring MFA, so password spraying is solved.' Only for accounts and flows the policies cover. Excluded service accounts, legacy protocols if not blocked, and service principals with secrets all sit outside it, and attackers spray exactly those.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
md: Baseline: few cloud-only admins on passkeys through PIM, restricted consent and reviewed apps, legacy auth and device code blocked, device-bound tokens where possible, hybrid bridges as Tier 0, and every log exported. Runbook: contain identities, hunt persistence in apps, devices and federation, scope data, evict at the root.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: A mitigation does not remove the bug. It removes one *route* from the bug to control. Patch the bug, prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and treat mitigations as the layer that protects you from the bugs you have not found yet.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results
md: ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Refinement says nothing about the steps the mapping hides. If the mapping ignores a variable that matters (say, durable state on disk), a wrong design can still refine the spec. Review the mapping as carefully as the spec.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision. Lesson 4 shows what that means for memory and speed, and the recipes that push FP8 into communication and optimizer state too.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
md: A fake quantizer reproduces a format's numerics, not its speed: what each value becomes after casting and scaling. Real hardware adds its own accumulation precision and order, so validate surprising results on the target GPU, but use the fake quantizer to test a recipe on your own tensors first.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions, the ones that need an understanding of the whole corpus.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: RLOO, GSPO, off-policy drift, and what RLVR teaches
md: Before trusting an RLVR gain: test on several model families (a Qwen-only result may be amplified priors), compare against random and format-only rewards, and compare against distilling a stronger model (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
md: A percentage in parentheses after a `perf stat` line, like `(74.98%)`, means that event ran only that fraction of the time and was scaled. Treat such numbers as estimates, and be most suspicious when the workload has phases.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
md: An enclave or TEE protects against software that cannot reach its memory. It does not remove side channels: if enclave code runs on the same core as the attacker, its cache footprint, branch history and timing are as observable as any other program's. Enclave code must still be constant-time.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: HTTP/2 framing, and how downgrading brings desync back
md: HTTP/2 removes framing ambiguity only while the request stays HTTP/2. Every downgrade to HTTP/1.1 must enforce RFC 9113's rules before writing text: content-length equals the DATA total, no connection-specific fields, no CR, LF or NUL in names or values.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Why BM25 and dense retrieval miss different documents
md: BM25 and dense retrieval fail on different documents. BM25 misses paraphrases; dense retrieval blurs exact identifiers, codes and rare names. Fusing the lists recovers documents either one would miss and promotes documents both agree on.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: IT protects data; OT protects people, equipment and the process. The order of priorities is different (safety and availability first), and every defence in this course is shaped by that.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
md: Stuxnet attacked at the two places defenders trusted most: the engineering software (so the program looked unchanged) and the operator's view (so the process looked normal). The defence is verification through a path the attacker does not control.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Federation replaces many passwords with one trust decision per app: accept whatever this IdP's key signs, after checking it was meant for me, now. Every attack in this course breaks one of those three parts: the key, the checks, or the moment.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
md: Treat the IdP's signing keys and the configuration that says which IdPs and keys are trusted as tier 0 (Microsoft's name for the assets that control every identity in an organisation): the same protection as domain controllers (the servers that hold Active Directory's accounts and keys). Anyone who can change either can become any user without touching a password.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: Identity governance answers: should this access exist, who decided, and can we prove it? Every entitlement should trace to a rule or an approved request, and the authoritative record (usually HR) drives the rest.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access workstations and the clean source rule
md: Session security cannot exceed device security. PAM, bastions and JIT protect the path; the PAW protects its start. Decide at a policy engine using identity, device and approval together, issue short-lived credentials, and enforce at one point.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu turns threshold selection into a 1D search over the histogram: maximize $\omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2$. It works well when changed and unchanged pixels form two separated groups, and only then.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
md: Isolating a host is not the same as stopping damage on it. NIST's example: a process that pings a remote host and, when the ping fails after disconnection, encrypts the disk. Capture what you need first when you can.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
md: Do not read the casino pair as "paying works". As one threat analyst quoted by The Register put it, the incidents are not necessarily comparable: we do not know their scope or which systems and backups were hit. And paying did not stop Caesars' data theft or its notification duties.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Parameterised queries: code and data on separate channels
md: Parameterise every value. Map every identifier and keyword through a fixed allowlist. Never quote a placeholder: in SQLite, `'?'` inside quotes is just a one-character string, and the call fails with "Incorrect number of bindings supplied"; Django's documentation warns against the same mistake with `'%s'`.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS (few I/O operations per second), bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input
md: Both V8 modes are experimental, and the blog says the fallback skips patterns with backreferences, lookarounds, large bounded repeats, or the `u` and `i` flags. Treat the flag as a safety net that you test with your own patterns, not as the fix. Rewriting and bounding input are the fixes.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Caching teacher outputs is only safe when the student's input is exactly the cached input. With random crops, flips, noise or mixup on the student side, cache the augmentation too or run the teacher live on the same batch. For language models the input is the token sequence itself, so the same rule says: teacher and student must score the same tokens.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones, which attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens) can be kept in the native dtype, the model's own number format.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
md: Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Deferring commitment is what let Coconut reach 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, while generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-written, product-specific configuration baselines with Level 1, Level 2 and STIG profiles. Each recommendation has a rationale, an audit check and a remediation, and maps to other frameworks, so one automated check can serve several auditors.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: Write rules for questions, give every rule a key, use auid>=1000 together with auid!=unset, write b32 and b64 rules on x86-64, put never rules first, keep syscall rules few, and end production rule sets with -e 2.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Every sensor has a layer it watches and layers it cannot. Syscall hooks miss io_uring; host tools miss userland rootkits; nothing on the host reliably reports its own removal. Combine kernel-side sensors at LSM or kprobe level with off-host silence alerts.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
md: Inventory, patch, baseline, sandbox, watch, rebuild. Each is ordinary engineering on its own; run together as a loop on every host, they turn a fleet from 2,000 separate risks into one system you can measure.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network. Also alert on deliberate blinding: Windows event 1102 (Security log cleared) and CloudTrail StopLogging or DeleteTrail calls are ATT&CK Defense Impairment techniques (T1685.005, T1685.002).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
md: Scanning finds what the list misses, and also things that are no longer true: exited processes and stale copies of live ones. A psscan-only entry with an exit time is history; one without an exit time whose PID is not in the list is the interesting case.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
md: Memory is where code without files, decrypted configs, live connections and the attacker's last commands live, and it is the first evidence to disappear. Capture it early, verify it, and trust only what two independent views agree on.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
md: Reordering is invisible to the thread that does it and visible to every other thread. Memory orderings are a portable contract about which reorderings other threads are allowed to observe.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
md: Hazard pointers: publish the address, fence, re-validate, then dereference. Retire into a private list and scan when it reaches R. Garbage is bounded by N x R even if threads stall.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: A common misconception: "if it didn't crash, it worked". An out-of-bounds write that lands in another variable usually does not crash at all. The program keeps running with corrupted data, which is often worse than crashing.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
md: Memory-safe languages do not make programs bug-free, but they turn the bug classes of this course from silent corruption into compile errors or clean crashes. About two thirds of severe bugs in big C and C++ codebases are memory bugs, so moving new code to memory-safe languages removes most of the worst bugs at the source.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Misconception: "no root detection" is automatically a finding. MASVS states that the absence of resilience measures "does not in itself constitute a vulnerability". It matters only when the profile includes MAS-R, for example to protect against fraud or cheating.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean
md: Misconception: "we use Face ID, so the data is protected by Face ID." Only if the data is encrypted under a key that requires it. If the token sits in UserDefaults or SharedPreferences, the prompt protects nothing from someone with the device's files (lesson 4) or a hook (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Checklist when porting MLA: normalize the latent only, and cache the normalized latent; rotate only $q^R$ and $k^R$, with the same pair layout as the checkpoint (interleaved here); scale scores by $1/\sqrt{d_h + d_h^R}$, times the YaRN factor for long-context checkpoints; and compare against the plain form before trusting any speedup.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield` (such as Rust's `std::thread::yield_now()`, which asks the operating system scheduler to run another thread for now). It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
md: Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP servers
